# The Research Compendium {#sec-compendium}

::: {.bookepigraph}
```{=latex}
\begin{flushright}\small
```
*The purpose of this article is to show how the R package
can be a suitable template for organizing files into a
research compendium to enhance the reproducibility of
research.*

[Marwick, Boettiger, and Mullen]{.smallcaps}, *Packaging
Data Analytical Work Reproducibly Using R (and Friends)*
(2018)
```{=latex}
\end{flushright}
```
:::

By the end of this chapter you will be able to look at
a folder of scripts and spreadsheets, name what kind of
research object it is trying to be, draw the line
between what counts as raw input and what counts as a
derived product, and say exactly which single build gate,
`R CMD check`, a tidy directory earns for free and what
that gate still leaves unexamined.



::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Before you start

**Reading time.** About 50 minutes.

**Prerequisites.** @sec-levels, for the L0-L3 ladder
vocabulary this chapter uses when it places a compendium
on it; no other chapter is assumed. Statistically, nothing
beyond reading a hazard ratio and a coefficient table, as
in the chapter's cohort and comorbidity examples, is
required. No R fluency beyond reading a short script and a
directory listing is assumed; this chapter writes almost
no code itself.

**By the end of this chapter you will be able to
answer:**

- Can you explain what a research compendium is, and
  trace its lineage from Gentleman and Temple Lang through
  `rrtools`?
- Can you justify why the R package is the compendium
  container, say precisely what `R CMD check` thereby
  checks, and say what it does not?
- Can you enumerate the [Five Pillars](glossary.qmd#gloss-the-five-pillars)
  of a compendium and
  name the single artifact that captures each?
- Can you distinguish the five compendium archetypes and
  state how their directory layout, their report, and
  their gates differ while the reproducibility machinery
  stays the same?
- Can you apply progressive disclosure to walk a project
  from one archetype to another without reorganizing it?

**Outline.**

- Orientation: a cohort analysis that is a scatter, not
  an object.
- The analyst's contribution: naming the archetype,
  fixing the raw-and-derived boundary, deciding what
  becomes a function.
- Where this sits on the stack: locatable, and nothing
  pinned yet.
- The compendium as the unit of reproducible work: where
  the idea comes from.
- The R package as the compendium container: `R CMD
  check` as a universal gate, and its limit.
- The Five Pillars.
- The directory layout, concretely.
- The five archetypes, each with a health-sciences
  example.
- Progressive disclosure: one layout, several stages.
- Worked example: one compendium through two archetypes.
- The cohort, continued: this book's own compendium
  against the Five Pillars.
:::

## Where this sits on the stack

This chapter captures nothing on the determinant stack
of @sec-levels in the sense of pinning a package version
or a system library; it captures the two layers that sit
above those, the analysis code and the input data,
by making them locatable and organized in the first
place. @fig-stack-compendium marks that: a compendium is
what first turns a scatter of files into something a
reader can find, name, and locate the raw-versus-derived
boundary within, which is the L0 rung and no further.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot_determinant_stack(
  captures = c('Analysis code', 'Input data'),
  title = 'The compendium captures locatability, not yet packages or environment')
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![The determinant stack of @sec-levels, with analysis code and input data marked as captured by this chapter. A research compendium does not pin a package version or an operating system; what it captures, for the first time, is that the code and the data are locatable, organized by convention, and separated into raw and derived, which is the L0 rung this chapter secures and the container the later chapters install L1 through L3 into.](03-research-compendium_files/figure-pdf/fig-stack-compendium-1.pdf){#fig-stack-compendium fig-pos='H' fig-alt='A horizontal bar chart of the nine-layer determinant stack, hardware at the bottom and intrinsic non-determinism at the top, each bar colored by the rung that secures it across the book. This chapter captures Analysis code, Input data; those layers are drawn at full color and, where validated, with a bordered outline. The remaining 7 layers are shown faded, for context, as secured elsewhere in the book.' width=1050}
:::
:::


## Orientation

Consider a first-year epidemiology student who has spent
three months on a cohort analysis: an incident-diabetes
study drawn from a registry, with a cleaning script, a
handful of models, four figures, and a draft of a
results section. The work exists, but it exists as a
scatter. The cleaning script sits in a downloads folder,
the models in a second file that reads a spreadsheet
whose path is hard-coded to one laptop, the figures as
loose `png` files pasted by hand into a manuscript, and
the record of which package versions produced any of it
nowhere at all. Nothing here is wrong as statistics. The
problem is that the analysis is not an object. It cannot
be handed to a colleague, cited, archived, or re-run,
because there is no single thing to hand over.

The remedy is to make the analysis one object. A
*research compendium* is that object: a single,
self-describing directory that bundles the code, the
data, the prose, and the record of the environment in
which the analysis was run, organized by convention so
that another person, or the same person a year later,
can find every part and regenerate the result. The
compendium is the third of the recurring ideas of this
book, after the levels ladder and the
capture-versus-validate distinction, and it is the one
that gives the other two something to act on. A
reproducibility level is a property *of* a compendium; a
validation gate is a check run *against* a compendium.

The compendium also sets the starting rung on the
ladder. Merely by being a version-controlled directory
whose parts can be located, a compendium reaches L0,
locatable. It is not yet L1, because nothing has pinned
the package versions. It is not yet L2, because nothing
has pinned the environment. And it is certainly not yet
L3, because nothing has re-run it and shown the numbers
to match a recorded baseline. What the compendium provides is the container
into which the later chapters install those higher
guarantees. We build the box first, and the chapters
that follow fill it.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what the scatter is missing

The epidemiology student's three months of work already
contains correct statistics. What, precisely, does the
compendium add that the statistics alone do not supply?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Not correctness, which the statistics already have, but
the property of being a single, locatable object: a thing
that can be handed to a colleague, cited, archived, and
re-run, because every part of it (the code, the data, and
eventually the environment record) lives in one
self-describing directory rather than scattered across a
laptop's folders and a manuscript's pasted figures.
:::
:::

## The analyst's contribution

Three judgments at the center of this chapter are the
analyst's alone. No tool scaffolds them, and getting
them wrong produces a tidy directory that is
nonetheless the wrong shape for the work.

1. **Naming the archetype.** The analyst must decide
   what kind of object the project is: a data analysis,
   a manuscript, a reusable package, a simulation study,
   or a blog. This choice governs the layout, whether a
   report is rendered, and which gates apply. It is a
   statement of intent, not a technical setting, and it
   is the organizing decision of the chapter.

2. **Fixing the raw-and-derived boundary.** The analyst
   must decide what is an immutable input and what is a
   product of the analysis. A file placed in
   `raw_data/` is a promise that it will never be
   modified; a file in `derived_data/` is a promise that
   it can always be regenerated from the raw inputs and
   the code. No program can draw this line, because it
   depends on where the analyst judges the science to
   begin.

3. **Deciding what becomes a function.** The analyst
   must decide which code is a throwaway pipeline step,
   belonging in `analysis/scripts/`, and which is a
   reusable procedure worth documenting and testing,
   belonging in `R/`. This judgment determines what
   `R CMD check` and the test suite will actually
   protect, and it is revisited continuously as a
   project matures.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: three judgments, one tool-free

A newcomer asks which of `zzcollab`'s commands tells the
analyst where the raw-and-derived boundary falls. What is
the honest answer?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

None of them. The framework's commands create the
directories (`raw_data/`, `derived_data/`) and enforce the
gates once the boundary is drawn, but drawing it, like
naming the archetype and deciding what becomes a function,
is a judgment about the science, not a setting the tooling
can infer from the files themselves.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## The vocabulary of this chapter

- **Research compendium.** A single self-describing
  directory bundling the code, data, prose, and
  environment record of an analysis, organized by
  convention so that it can be located and re-run.
- **R-package skin.** The minimal set of files
  (`DESCRIPTION`, `NAMESPACE`, an `R/` directory) that
  makes a directory a valid R package, and therefore
  checkable by the R build tools.
- **`R CMD check`.** The standard R command that builds
  a package, runs its tests, and applies dozens of
  standardized checks; here it serves as a universal
  integrity gate on the compendium's package skin
  (`R/`, the tests, `DESCRIPTION`). It does not check
  `analysis/`, which the build excludes.
- **The Five Pillars.** The five artifacts a compendium
  manages, one per capture point: the `Dockerfile`,
  `renv.lock`, `.Rprofile`, the source code, and the
  data.
- **Archetype.** The kind of research object a
  compendium is (data analysis, manuscript, package,
  simulation study, or blog), which varies the layout
  and the gates but not the underlying machinery.
- **Render gate.** A validation check that a report or
  document rebuilds cleanly from source; it applies to
  archetypes that carry a report and not to those that
  do not.
- **Raw versus derived data.** Immutable original
  inputs versus the processed datasets regenerated from
  them by code.
- **Progressive disclosure.** The property that one
  layout supports a project's evolution from one
  archetype to another with no reorganization.
:::

## The compendium as the unit of reproducible work

The idea is not new, and its history is worth a
paragraph because it explains the shape of the modern
object. Gentleman and Temple Lang, writing in 2007,
proposed the compendium in its current sense: a document
that combines text, code, and data in a form a reader
can actually execute, rather than a paper that merely
describes an analysis performed elsewhere
[@gentleman2007]. The proposal drew on Knuth's earlier
notion of [literate programming](glossary.qmd#gloss-literate-programming),
in which prose and code
are woven into one source [@knuth1984]. For some years
the compendium remained an aspiration without a
conventional implementation. Peng, arguing that
reproducibility should be treated as a minimum standard
for computational science, sharpened the motivation
without settling the container [@peng2011].

The decisive move came from Marwick, Boettiger, and
Mullen, who observed that a container of exactly the
required shape already existed and was in daily use by
thousands of R developers: the R package
[@marwick2018]. An R package, as standardized by Wickham
[@wickham2015], already provides a `DESCRIPTION` file
recording metadata and dependencies, an `R/` directory
for reusable functions, a `tests/` directory for unit
tests, a `vignettes/` directory for long-form prose, and
a rigorously specified build system. Marwick and
colleagues extended this layout with a single top-level
`analysis/` directory holding subdirectories for raw
data, derived data, scripts, figures, and the manuscript
itself, and packaged the whole as the `rrtools` tool.
The resulting compendium can be installed, tested, and
checked with the very same commands used for any R
package. Nust, Boettiger, and Marwick later wrote a
companion guide on how to *read* such a compendium, which
is a useful sign that the object had matured enough to
have a reading protocol at all [@nust2018].

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: why the R package, not a new format

Marwick, Boettiger, and Mullen could have proposed a
wholly new compendium format instead of reusing the R
package. What did reusing an existing format buy that a
bespoke one would not have?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

A build system, a validation tool, and tens of thousands
of developers already fluent in the convention, all for
free. A bespoke format would have needed its own checker
written from scratch and its own community taught to use
it; the R package came with `R CMD check` and a working
ecosystem already attached.
:::
:::

## The R package as the compendium container

The choice of the R package as the container is the
single most consequential design decision in this
lineage, and it repays careful statement. It appears at
first to be a convenience, reuse of a familiar layout,
but its real value is that it makes an existing,
rigorous, and universal gate apply to the compendium's
package skin for free. What that gate does not reach
matters as much as what it does, and we state both.

The gate is `R CMD check`. When R was designed as a
system for distributing statistical software, its
authors built a command that takes a package and subjects
it to dozens of standardized checks: that the code parses and
loads, that every documented function matches its
documentation, that declared dependencies are actually
available, that the examples run, and that the tests
pass. The command was built to keep the tens of thousands
of packages on CRAN mutually consistent. By dressing a
compendium in the R-package skin, one inherits this
entire apparatus at no cost. A compendium that passes
`R CMD check` is one whose functions in `R/` load, whose
stated dependencies resolve, and whose tests succeed, in a
clean process that carries none of the author's
accumulated and undeclared state.

The qualification 'in `R/`' is exact, not cautious.
`R CMD check` does not check the directory it is pointed
at; it checks the package tarball that `R CMD build`
makes from that directory, and the build omits every path
listed in `.Rbuildignore`. A compendium lists `^analysis$`
there, as it must, because raw data, derived files, and a
manuscript do not belong in an installable package. The
consequence is that the check never sees `analysis/`. An
analysis script with a syntax error, or one that calls
`library()` on a package declared nowhere, passes
`R CMD check` with no error, warning, or note. The same
undeclared package used inside
a function in `R/` draws a WARNING ('`::` or `:::` import
not declared from'). The code in `analysis/` therefore
needs gates of its own: a render gate, which executes it,
and a dependency scan, which reads it for packages that
the lockfile does not pin. Both are developed in
@sec-verification.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Verification

To see the claim hold: add a deliberate syntax error to
any script under `analysis/scripts/`, then run
`rcmdcheck::rcmdcheck('.')` (we ran this on a toy
compendium with R 4.6.1 and `rcmdcheck` 1.4.0) from the
project root. It reports zero errors, warnings, or notes,
because the broken file never entered the build. To make
the same claim fail on purpose, move the broken code, or a
function that calls an undeclared package, into a file
under `R/` instead, and run the check again; it now fails
or warns, because that file is part of what gets built.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall

A new compendium that omits `^analysis$` from
`.Rbuildignore`, or deletes the line while editing the
file by hand, does not fail quietly. `R CMD build` then
tries to fold the raw data, the derived files, and the
rendered report into the installable tarball, which can
make the build slow, bloat the package beyond what CRAN
or a reviewer will tolerate, or fail outright on a binary
data file the build process cannot parse as package data.
The fix is to treat `.Rbuildignore` as part of the
package skin, checked into version control like
`DESCRIPTION`, not as an incidental dotfile.
:::

This is why the R-package structure is not incidental to
the compendium but constitutive of it. Every archetype we
shall meet below, however different in outward shape,
carries the same minimal R-package skin, and therefore
`R CMD check` is the one gate that applies to all of
them. A manuscript compendium adds a render gate on top;
a simulation compendium adds a seeding discipline; a
package compendium leans on the check most heavily of
all; but the universal floor is the same. It is a floor
under `R/` and the tests, not under the analysis, which
is one reason the analyst's third judgment, what becomes
a function, matters: code moved into `R/` comes under the
check, and code left in `analysis/` does not. We return
to this point when we tabulate the archetypes, because it
is the thread that unifies them.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: why an R package?

A colleague proposes to organize a compendium as a plain
folder with sensible subdirectory names, arguing that the
R-package files (`DESCRIPTION`, `NAMESPACE`) are empty
ceremony for an analysis that is not a package anyone will
install. What is lost by this choice?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The plain folder can still be locatable and can still
hold all five artifacts, so it can in principle reach the
higher levels of the ladder. What is lost is the universal
gate. Without the R-package skin, `R CMD check` has
nothing to check, so there is no single, standard,
pre-built command that verifies the functions load, their
dependencies resolve, and the tests pass. (The analysis
scripts are a separate matter: with or without the skin,
they need a render gate and a dependency scan.) The analyst
must then assemble an equivalent set of checks by hand for
every project. The ceremony is precisely the interface
that makes an existing verification apparatus apply.
:::
:::

## The Five Pillars

A compendium is defined by convention, but it *manages* a
specific and small set of artifacts. The `zzcollab`
framework organizes these as the Five Pillars: the five
things a compendium reads, writes, and version-controls,
one for each point at which reproducibility can be
captured [@thomas2026zzcollab]. An analysis is reproducible only
to the extent that all five are captured, and the pillars
are layered rather than independent, each resting on the
ones beneath it.

1. **Computational environment**, captured by the
   `Dockerfile`. This pillar fixes the operating system,
   the R version itself, the system libraries, and the
   document toolchain, all the software beneath the R
   packages. It is the subject of @sec-containers.

2. **Package versions**, captured by `renv.lock`. This
   pillar records the exact version of every R package the
   analysis loads, so that the same set can be restored on
   another machine. It is the subject of
   @sec-dependencies.

3. **Session configuration**, captured by the project
   `.Rprofile`. This pillar fixes the R options, the
   random-number-generator kind, the locale and timezone,
   and the thread counts that shape a session before any
   user code runs.

4. **Source code**, captured by the version-control
   history. This pillar holds the scripts, the functions,
   the manuscript source, and the tests that implement the
   analysis.

5. **Data**, captured either by inclusion in the
   compendium, for small redistributable files, or by
   reference to an external repository with a resolvable
   identifier, for large or restricted data.

Two of the pillars are not coordinate with the other
three. Source code and data, pillars four and five, are
the inputs whose re-execution is the goal; the
environment, packages, and session, pillars one through
three, are the conditions under which that re-execution
occurs. This chapter is about the container that holds all
five and the shape that container takes. The individual
pillars are developed in the chapters named against them.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: layered, not independent

Why does the chapter say the pillars are 'layered rather
than independent,' and what would it mean to capture
pillar two, package versions, while leaving pillar one,
the computational environment, uncaptured?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

A lockfile restored outside any pinned environment still
depends on whatever R version and system libraries the
host machine happens to supply, so pillar two's guarantee,
'the same packages,' is only as strong as pillar one's,
'the same environment,' lets it be. Capturing packages
without the environment is exactly @sec-levels's L1
without L2: a real step, but one whose benefit a different
R release or a missing system library can still erase.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## The honest level

This chapter's own practice stops at naming and separating
the five artifacts; it leaves their actual capture, and the
rung that capture buys, to the chapters named against each
pillar above.
:::

## The directory layout, concretely

It helps to see the whole layout at once. The following
is the top-level structure of a `zzcollab` compendium.
The block is illustrative and is not executed.

```
penguin-analysis/
├── DESCRIPTION           # package metadata and dependencies
├── NAMESPACE             # generated; exported functions
├── LICENSE
├── R/                    # reusable, documented functions
├── man/                  # generated function documentation
├── tests/                # tinytest runner
├── inst/tinytest/        # unit tests (test-*.R)
├── vignettes/            # long-form prose
├── analysis/
│   ├── data/
│   │   ├── raw_data/       # immutable inputs
│   │   ├── derived_data/   # regenerable script outputs
│   │   └── metadata/       # data dictionaries, provenance
│   ├── scripts/           # numbered pipeline steps
│   ├── report/            # report.Rmd / index.qmd manuscript
│   ├── figures/           # generated figures
│   └── tables/            # generated tables
├── Dockerfile            # Pillar 1: environment
├── renv.lock             # Pillar 2: package versions
├── .Rprofile             # Pillar 3: session configuration
├── Makefile              # workflow entry points
├── zzcollab.yaml         # configuration: base image, archetype
├── .zzcollab-state       # generated state record; never hand-edited
└── .github/workflows/    # continuous-integration definitions
```

The reader will note the division. Above the `analysis/`
directory sits the standard R-package machinery: this is
the skin that makes `R CMD check` apply. Within
`analysis/` sits the research proper, in the Marwick
convention, with the raw-and-derived data separation that
is the analyst's second judgment made physical. At the
root sit the three environment artifacts, one per pillar,
alongside the `Makefile` that provides the commands and
the `zzcollab.yaml` that records, among a small set of
parameters, the archetype. That last file is our bridge
to the centerpiece of the chapter, because the archetype
is a first-class parameter recorded there, elicited at
creation time alongside the choice of base image.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: finding the boundary in the tree

Using the directory listing above, name the one line that
marks the boundary `R CMD check` actually respects, and
state which side of that line `renv.lock` falls on.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The boundary is the `analysis/` entry itself, the one path
`.Rbuildignore` excludes from the build. `renv.lock` sits
outside `analysis/`, at the project root, so it is not
excluded by that line, but it is also not parsed by
`R CMD check`, which reads `DESCRIPTION` for declared
dependencies rather than the lockfile; the two artifacts
answer different questions about the same package skin.
:::
:::

## The README and the data dictionary

The directory listing above names a `README` nowhere, and
that absence is not an oversight to copy. A compendium that
captures all five pillars perfectly but ships without a
`README` still fails the first test a stranger applies to
it, because the stranger has no entry point. The NHS RAP
Community of Practice makes the README the entire baseline
criterion for reproducibility, ahead of any of the five
pillars: a repository reaches the lowest rung only once it
'includes a README.md file (or equivalent) that clearly
details steps a user must follow to reproduce the code'
[@nhsrap2024]. A `README.md` at the project root should
state, in order, what the project is for, how to reproduce
it (the `make` target or `Rscript` command that runs the
pipeline end to end, and the archetype-specific gate from
@sec-levels that passing it claims), and where the data
dictionary lives for anyone who needs the columns rather
than the narrative.

The data dictionary is a second, separate document, usually
in `analysis/data/metadata/` or beside the extract it
describes, and it answers a question the README should not
try to: what is each column, exactly. At minimum it gives,
per column, the name, its type, a one-line meaning, its
units where numeric, and its provenance, meaning whether it
was measured, derived, or simulated and by what script. This
book's own `analysis/data/README.md` is a worked, if
unusually candid, example: because the extract it describes
is synthetic, the dictionary can also say outright which
rows are planted defects and why, a disclosure a real data
use agreement would instead replace with an access-control
statement. The columns table there (`mrn`, `patient_name`,
`hba1c`, and seven more, each with a type and a one-line
meaning) is the shape to imitate; the provenance section
above it, naming the exact generator script and seed, is the
part a real project cannot write the same way, since a real
extract's provenance is the originating system and the
extraction date, not a committed script.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: README versus data dictionary

A compendium's `README.md` says 'run `make all` to reproduce
every figure in the report' and nothing else about the data.
Is this README sufficient on its own, and what, if anything,
is still missing from the compendium?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The sentence satisfies the RAP baseline criterion by itself,
since it states the one command a user must run. What is
missing is not part of the README's job: a data dictionary
naming each column's type, meaning, units, and provenance.
A reproducer who can rerun the pipeline but cannot tell what
`hba1c` means or whether it was measured or simulated has not
been given a reproducible analysis, only a reproducible
button press.
:::
:::

## Project-oriented paths: `here`, not `setwd()`

A script that opens with `setwd('/Users/jane/project')`
reproduces on exactly one machine: Jane's. The fix taught by
the `here` package is to mark the project root once, with a
file such as `.here` or the marker RStudio and Git already
leave behind, and then build every path with `here::here()`,
which walks up from the working directory until it finds that
marker and returns paths relative to it from there on
[@bryan2024safepaths]. A script that reads
`here::here('analysis', 'data', 'raw_data', 'cohort_raw.csv')`
resolves the same file whether R is launched from the
project root, from `analysis/report/`, or from a continuous-
integration runner that checks the repository out to a
different absolute path each time, because the path is
computed from the marker rather than typed as a string.

This book's own chapters, inspected directly, show why the
discipline matters even without `setwd()`. Several chapters
reach the cohort extract with `'../data/raw_data/...'`, but
`08-testing-quality.qmd` reaches the same file with
`'../../analysis/data/raw_data/...'`, two directories deeper,
because that chunk assumes a different starting working
directory than the others do. Every one of these paths works
only because the author tracked, chunk by chunk, how many
`../` steps the renderer's working directory is from the
target file; `here::here('analysis', 'data', 'raw_data',
'cohort_raw.csv')` would resolve identically from any of
these chunks, because it does not depend on the renderer's
starting point at all. The relative-path convention is not
wrong, exactly; it is fragile in a way that is invisible
until a chunk is moved, copied into a different chapter, or
run from a different tool.

## The five archetypes

We come now to the heart of the matter, and to the point
this book returns to in every chapter: a research
compendium is not only a manuscript. It is tempting, once
one has seen the `analysis/report/` directory, to imagine
that the purpose of a compendium is always to render a
paper. This is the common case, but it is one case among
five, and treating it as the whole is the error the
present section exists to prevent.

`zzcollab` treats the research archetype as a first-class
initialization parameter, orthogonal to the choice of
computational environment [@thomas2026zzcollab]. Where the base
image fixes the environment, the archetype determines the
starting scaffolding: the directory emphasis, whether a
primary report exists, and which validation gates apply on
top of the universal one. Five archetypes are advertised.
Because every one of them carries the minimal
R-package skin, `R CMD check` remains the universal gate
across all five, as the framework's own whitepaper stresses
in its account of the archetype axis. What varies is not
the reproducibility machinery, which is identical, but the
shape of the work and the gates it warrants. We take each
in turn, with a health-sciences example, and then tabulate
the differences.

### 1. Data analysis (a cohort study)

The first archetype is the exploratory and confirmatory
data analysis with no manuscript as its primary organizing
document. This is the closest to the original `rrtools`
use case, and it is the archetype of the epidemiology
student of our orientation. The work lives in
`analysis/scripts/`, as numbered pipeline steps, and in
`analysis/figures/`, with the derived datasets in
`analysis/data/derived_data/`. Consider an
incident-diabetes cohort study: a cleaning script that
reads the registry extract from `raw_data/` and writes an
analysis-ready table to `derived_data/`, a modeling
script that fits a Cox proportional-hazards model and
writes the coefficient table to `tables/`, and a plotting
script that writes the Kaplan-Meier curves to `figures/`.
There may be a short results document, but it is not the
point; the point is the pipeline and its outputs.

The applicable gates are the universal `R CMD check` and
the unit tests, the latter guarding the cleaning logic and
the data invariants (that the cohort has the expected
number of subjects, and that a derived rate matches a
value recorded in a baseline file within a stated
tolerance, rather than merely falling in a plausible
range). A
render gate is optional here, because there may be no
report to render. The reproducibility machinery,
environment and packages and session, is nonetheless
present in full.

### 2. Scholarly manuscript (a comorbidity paper)

The second archetype makes the manuscript the organizing
principle. A `report.Rmd` or `index.qmd` file in
`analysis/report/` is created on day one and written in
parallel with the analysis, so that the prose and the
numbers never drift apart. Every figure in the paper is
regenerated on each render, rather than pasted in by hand. A
representative deployment is a study of the comorbidity of
PTSD, depression, and diabetes among Black women drawn from
a trauma-study cohort, using variable selection, multiple
imputation, and causal mediation analysis. The compendium
organizes the manuscript in `analysis/report/report.Rmd`,
the statistical functions in `R/` with `roxygen2`
documentation, the analysis pipeline in
`analysis/scripts/`, and the imputed datasets in
`analysis/data/derived_data/`.

Here the render gate is central, not optional: a
validation run rebuilds the report from source, and a
failure to render is a failure of the compendium. The gates
are therefore `R CMD check`, the unit tests, and the render
of `report.Rmd` to PDF. This is the archetype most readers
imagine when they hear the word compendium, and the burden
of the present section is that it is only the second of
five.

### 3. R package (a summary-table package)

The third archetype arises when the reusable code matures
into something of general interest, at which point `R/`,
`man/`, and `tests/` become the first-class content and the
compendium is shareable as a CRAN-style package. The
distinguishing feature, and the reason this archetype
matters for the argument, is that *there is no report to
render at all*. A package that generates
publication-quality clinical-trial summary tables has no
manuscript as its deliverable; its
deliverable is the exported, documented, tested function. A
representative deployment is exactly such a summary-table
package, hosting its source in `R/`, its examples in
`vignettes/`, and its
documentation as a generated website.

The gates for this archetype are `R CMD check`, run at its
full strength, and the unit tests. There is no render gate,
because there is nothing to render. This case is the
clearest refutation of the manuscript-only view: an
entirely valid, fully reproducible compendium can produce
no report whatsoever, and its integrity rests on the
universal check and the tests alone.

### 4. Simulation study (a power analysis)

The fourth archetype is the simulation study: a power
calculation, or an assessment of the operating
characteristics of a proposed trial design, in which the
compendium enumerates a grid of parameter configurations,
runs Monte Carlo replicates at each, and stores the
results. The layout leans on `analysis/scripts/` for the
simulation driver and on `analysis/data/derived_data/` for
the stored replicate results, which are treated as derived
data because they can be regenerated from the code and the
seeds.

The distinguishing discipline of this archetype is
*seeding*. A simulation whose random draws are not pinned
by an explicit `set.seed()` is not reproducible even in
principle, because a second run produces different numbers
by construction. The archetype therefore emphasizes
explicit seeding and parallel execution, and a
recommended practice is to store a seed column alongside
the parameter grid so that each replicate is individually
reproducible. Consider a power simulation for a
longitudinal trial: the driver builds a grid over sample
size and effect size, assigns each row an integer seed,
simulates a dataset for each row, fits the planned model,
and records whether the null was rejected. The empirical
power is then the rejection rate within each cell. The
gates are `R CMD check`, the unit tests, and, as an
emphasis particular to this archetype, a test that the
seeded simulation returns identical output on a second
call. A render gate is optional, since the deliverable is
often the stored results rather than a paper.

### 5. Blog (a teaching notebook)

The fifth archetype is the blog or lab notebook, in which
the compendium renders, in the general case, not one report
but many documents. A
teaching blog carrying a series of methods posts, or a
running lab notebook of analyses, is a single compendium
whose `analysis/` tree may hold many `index.qmd` files,
each rendered to a static site by the same machinery that
renders a manuscript. The framework's representative
deployment is the limiting case of a single post. Integration with Quarto
[@allaire2024]
enables publication to the site from the same compendium
that produced the underlying analyses, so that the full
five-pillar reproducibility stack applies to web-published
teaching content without any change to the workflow.

The gate here is again the universal `R CMD check`, joined
by a render gate that must succeed for *each* post the
compendium carries rather than for a single report. The
multiplicity is the distinguishing feature of the general
case: a blog compendium is a
render-many, where the manuscript is a render-one and the
package is a render-none. The machinery beneath all three
is, once more, identical.

The five archetypes and their differences are summarized
in @tbl-archetypes, and @fig-gates shows which validation
gates apply to each. The reader should read both across the
rows, to see how the layout and the gates vary, and down
the two universal columns, to see how much stays fixed.


::: {#tbl-archetypes .cell tbl-cap='The five research-compendium archetypes. The reproducibility machinery is identical across all five; only the directory emphasis, the presence of a rendered report, and the gates that apply on top of the universal R CMD check differ.'}

## Check your understanding: the render-none case

A reviewer objects that a compendium producing no rendered
document cannot be a reproducible research object, since
there is no result to reproduce. Which archetype answers
this objection, and how?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The R-package archetype answers it. A package that exports
a summary-table function has no report to render, yet it is
fully reproducible: its result is the behavior of the
function, and that behavior is protected by `R CMD check`
and by the unit tests, which regenerate and verify the
function's outputs on every check. The absence of a render
gate does not weaken reproducibility; it simply reflects
that the deliverable is a tested procedure rather than a
document. Reproducibility is a property of re-execution,
not of rendering.
:::
:::

## How each archetype treats the chapters ahead

The reproducibility machinery is identical across the five
archetypes; only its weight shifts. @tbl-archetype-weight
is the reference every later chapter points back to rather
than restates: for each archetype, how the ladder reads it
(@sec-levels), how heavily it leans on a
[sealed render](glossary.qmd#gloss-sealed-render)
(@sec-literate), which kind of test carries its weight
(@sec-testing), how its continuous-integration gates are
configured (@sec-verification), how much a pipeline tool
earns its keep (@sec-pipelines), and how it is ultimately
shared (@sec-archiving).

| Archetype | Ladder (@sec-levels) | Literate programming (@sec-literate) | Testing (@sec-testing) | CI gates (@sec-verification) | Pipeline (@sec-pipelines) | Sharing (@sec-archiving) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Data analysis | Same rungs as a manuscript; L3 via a baseline on a derived rate | Light; an internal HTML summary, not a typeset report | Leans on data-validation and reproducibility tests | Render gate only if a report exists | Most valuable case for `targets`; re-run constantly | Deposited as itself |
| Scholarly manuscript | Full apparatus; L3 compares tables and figures with recorded baselines | Center of gravity; the sealed render this chapter is built around | Adds a report-renders-and-matches-baseline test | Render gate is central, not optional | Modest; often a one-target build around the sealed report | Deposited beside the article it supports |
| R package | L2 via `R CMD check` and tests in a clean rebuild; L3 via a baseline on function output | Largely absent; help pages and vignettes stand in | Native home of unit testing; `R CMD check` runs the suite | No render gate unless a vignette exists | None; `R CMD check` plays the corresponding role | Also released to CRAN or an R-universe, not only archived |
| Simulation study | L2 is nominal without the seed discipline; RNG kind is the load-bearing determinant | Thin; a presentation layer over pre-computed, stored results | Leans hardest on the seed-determinism test | A reduced, fixed-seed grid runs under CI; the full grid runs elsewhere | Strongest case; `targets` branching maps the parameter grid | Recorded seeds and the union lockfile are what a re-runner needs |
| Blog | Applies post by post; L3 needs a baseline per post | Central but multiplied across many rendered posts | Tests the code each post's examples depend on | Render gate iterates over every post | Rebuilds only the posts whose sources changed | Deployed as a website; the compendium behind it is still deposited |

## Progressive disclosure

The five archetypes are not walls between separate kinds
of project. They are, rather, stages a single project may
pass through, and the framework's most useful structural
property is that the same layout supports the whole
trajectory without reorganization. This is what the
framework calls *progressive disclosure*: the same
directory layout, the same `Makefile`, and the same Five
Pillars carry a project from one archetype to the next.
No transition demands that the analyst tear the
project apart and rebuild it in a new shape.

The trajectory is easy to picture, and it is the one our
epidemiology student is likely to walk. The project begins
as a data analysis: scripts and figures, no manuscript. As
the findings firm up, a `report.Rmd` is added to
`analysis/report/` and the project becomes a manuscript
compendium, with the render gate now active, but nothing
already written needs to move. In the course of the
analysis a cleaning routine and a modeling helper prove
useful enough to document and test, so they migrate from
`analysis/scripts/` into `R/`. The package archetype's
gates begin to bite on them without any change to the
layout. Should one of those functions reach general
interest, the compendium can be shared as a package, its
`R/` and `man/` and `tests/` now first-class, while the
`analysis/` directory recedes to a development notebook.
The same compendium has been, in turn, a data analysis, a
manuscript, and a package, and at no point was it
reorganized.

The lesson we draw, and it is the organizing lesson of the
chapter, is that the archetype is a description of a
project's current emphasis rather than a permanent
category. The reproducibility machinery is invariant across
the archetypes and across the transitions between them. It
is precisely this invariance that lets a project evolve
without ever leaving the reproducible state it started in.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what moves, what does not

In the student's trajectory above, name one thing that
changes at each transition and one thing that never does.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

What changes: the archetype recorded in `zzcollab.yaml`,
and the set of gates that apply (a render gate joins at
the manuscript transition; `R CMD check`'s documentation
and export checks start to bite once functions migrate
into `R/`). What never changes: the directory layout
itself. No file already written is moved or renamed at
either transition, and the Five Pillars sit in the same
three root-level artifacts throughout.
:::
:::

## Worked example

To make the progressive-disclosure trajectory concrete, we
follow a single compendium through its first two
archetypes, staying at the level of the directory and the
gates rather than the analysis. Suppose our student begins
the incident-diabetes study. The compendium is created and
its archetype recorded as a data analysis. The shell
session below is illustrative and is not executed.

```bash
$ mkdir diabetes-cohort && cd diabetes-cohort
$ zzc analysis  # tidyverse base-image profile; archetype set separately
```

The student places the registry extract under `raw_data/`,
writes `analysis/scripts/01_clean.R` to produce a derived
cohort table, and writes `analysis/scripts/02_model.R` to
fit the Cox model. A unit test in `inst/tinytest/` asserts
the cohort size and that the fitted hazard ratio matches a
value recorded in a committed baseline file, within a
stated tolerance, which is a test that can actually fail
if the model's inputs or the `survival` version drift,
unlike a bound such as 'no hazard ratio is negative' that
every correct and every broken fit alike would satisfy. At
this point the only gates that apply are the
universal check and the tests, run in a clean environment:

```bash
$ make check-renv     # dependencies declared and locked
$ make docker-test    # tinytest only
$ make docker-check   # R CMD check
```

Some weeks later the results are firm enough to write up.
The student adds `analysis/report/report.Rmd`, moving the
figure code out of `02_model.R` and into report chunks that
regenerate the figures on render. The compendium is now a
manuscript, and the archetype line in `zzcollab.yaml` is
updated to reflect it, but not a single existing file has
moved. A render gate now joins the others:

```bash
$ make docker-render  # rebuild report.Rmd to PDF
```

The cleaning routine, meanwhile, has grown into a general
helper worth documenting, so it migrates from
`analysis/scripts/01_clean.R` into `R/prepare_cohort.R`,
gains a `roxygen2` block, and picks up its own unit tests.
The package archetype's discipline now protects it, and
`R CMD check` verifies that the documentation matches the
function signature. The same compendium is now doing the
work of three archetypes at once, on one unchanged layout,
with each gate applying to the part of the project that
warrants it. This is progressive disclosure in operation,
and it is the payoff of having chosen a single, principled
container at the outset.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: the manuscript transition

When `report.Rmd` is added and the project becomes a
manuscript compendium, what single gate becomes active
that was not before, and what about the compendium's
Five Pillars status is unaffected by this transition?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The render gate becomes active: a validation run must now
rebuild `report.Rmd` to PDF, where before there was no
report to render. The Five Pillars are unaffected, because
adding a manuscript changes which gates apply, not which
artifacts capture the environment, the packages, the
session, the code, or the data; those five pillars are the
same five files or records before and after the archetype
changes.
:::
:::

## The cohort, continued

The chapters placed so far have all described a composite
student's compendium. Here is the same classification
exercise performed on this book's own running cohort
compendium, as it actually sits in this repository today.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
raw <- load_cohort('../data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv')
cohort <- clean_cohort(raw)
pillars <- c(
  environment_dockerfile = file.exists('../../Dockerfile'),
  packages_renv_lock = file.exists('../../renv.lock'),
  session_rprofile = file.exists('../../.Rprofile'),
  source_code_r_cohort = file.exists('../../R/cohort.R'),
  data_raw_csv = file.exists('../data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv')
)
pillars
#> environment_dockerfile     packages_renv_lock       session_rprofile 
#>                  FALSE                  FALSE                   TRUE 
#>   source_code_r_cohort           data_raw_csv 
#>                   TRUE                   TRUE
nrow(raw)
#> [1] 338
nrow(cohort)
#> [1] 337
```
:::


Three of the Five Pillars already have an artifact in this
repository: the project `.Rprofile` (session configuration),
`R/cohort.R` (source code, under version control), and the
raw extract itself (data, included directly because it is
small and synthetic). Two do not: there is no `Dockerfile`
and no `renv.lock` at the time this chapter is being
written, so the environment and the package-versions
pillars are uncaptured. Against the archetype table above,
this compendium is a **data analysis**, since its deliverable
is the pipeline of `R/cohort.R` and the chunks this book's
chapters run against it, not a rendered manuscript of its
own; the applicable gates are therefore the universal
`R CMD check` and the unit tests, with no render gate
required. Measured against the Five Pillars rather than the
archetype table, three artifacts present and two absent is
consistent with @sec-levels's own placement of this same
compendium at L0, locatable, and no further: having a
source-code pillar and a data pillar is exactly what makes
a compendium locatable, and it is not yet what pins a
package version or an environment.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: pillars present, rung reached

This compendium currently has three of the Five Pillars
captured by an artifact (session, source code, data) and
two absent (environment, packages). Does having three of
five pillars put it partway between L0 and L1 on the
ladder of @sec-levels?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

No. The ladder is not a count of pillars; it is a
cumulative scale in which L1 specifically requires the
package-versions pillar (`renv.lock`) and L2 specifically
requires the environment pillar (`Dockerfile`). Having
the session, source-code, and data pillars without a
lockfile still leaves the compendium at L0, because L0
asks only that the source and data be locatable under
version control, which all three present pillars already
satisfy, and no rung is reached by partial credit across
unrelated pillars.
:::
:::

## Collaborating with an LLM

A language model is a capable assistant for scaffolding and
organizing a compendium, and an unreliable one for the
judgments that define it. The three triples below mark the
division.

::: {.callout-important}
## Restricted data

A compendium's own directory listing can be enough to
tempt a reader into pasting what it names (habit 3). Never
paste or upload protected health information, identifiable
records, or data covered by a data-use agreement, nor
outputs derived from them, into a model unless your
institution has approved that endpoint for that data;
describe the structure instead, as the prompts below do,
with file names, column names and types, and a synthetic
example. A coding agent reads the files in the directory it
is started in, so run one only in a compendium whose data
it is permitted to see.
:::

**Prompt.** 'I have a folder of R scripts and CSV files for
a cohort analysis. Propose a research-compendium directory
structure and tell me which files go where.'

*Watch for*: a plausible layout that silently guesses the
raw-and-derived boundary, placing a file the model cannot
distinguish as input or output into the wrong directory,
and an omission of the R-package skin (`DESCRIPTION`,
`NAMESPACE`) that quietly forfeits the `R CMD check` gate.

*Verification*: confirm by hand that every file in
`raw_data/` is a genuine immutable input and every file in
`derived_data/` is regenerable from code, because this is
the analyst's judgment and not the model's. Confirm the
R-package skin is present, and run `R CMD check` to
establish that the proposed structure is in fact checkable,
remembering that the check covers `R/` and the tests, not
the scripts under `analysis/`.

**Prompt.** 'Which archetype should this project be, and
which validation gates apply?'

*Watch for*: a default to the manuscript archetype, since
that is the most common case in the model's training data,
even when the project has no report and is really a package
or a simulation study; and a confident enumeration of gates
that includes a render gate for a project that renders
nothing.

*Verification*: decide the archetype yourself from the
project's actual deliverable, a document, a function, or a
set of stored simulation results, and then check that the
gates the model lists match @tbl-archetypes for that
archetype. A render gate on a render-none package is the
tell that the model has guessed the archetype wrongly.

**Prompt.** 'Write the unit tests that should gate this
compendium.'

*Watch for*: tests that assert only that functions exist or
that a script runs without error, which are structural
checks rather than correctness tests, and, for a simulation
compendium, an absence of any test that the seeded output
is reproducible.

*Verification*: read each generated test and confirm it
checks a value the analysis actually depends on, not merely
that code executes. For a simulation study, add or verify a
test that compares the seeded output with a baseline
recorded in an earlier session and committed, within a
stated tolerance (@sec-testing), since that is the
property the archetype exists to protect and the one a
model is most likely to omit. A second call in the same
session agrees with the first even when the generator has
changed, so it does not test this.

## Solutions

Attempt an exercise before expanding its solution. The first
two work on an analysis of the reader's own, so what they
produce will vary; the boxes say what a good answer
establishes.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 1

No single correct answer. What a good answer establishes is
that the classification follows from the **deliverable**,
not from the subject matter or the size of the project.

The discriminating question is what the project is *for*.
If the answer is a paper, it is a scholarly manuscript and
the render gate applies. If it is a set of results with no
document, it is a data analysis and the render gate may or
may not apply. If it is a function other people will call,
it is an R package and the render gate does not apply at
all. If it is an estimate of an operating characteristic
obtained by repeated sampling, it is a simulation study and
the seed-determinism gate applies. If it is a post, it is a
blog.

The gates on top of the universal `R CMD check` are drawn
from a short list: unit tests, which apply universally; the
render gate, which applies where a document is the
deliverable; and seed determinism, which applies where the
result is stochastic. Naming a gate that does not apply is
as much the point of the exercise as naming one that does,
since the chapter's claim is that the machinery is
identical and only the gates differ.

A reader who finds their analysis is genuinely two
archetypes, a manuscript that also ships a reusable
function, has found the ordinary case rather than an
anomaly, and should apply the union of the gates.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 2

No single correct answer. What a good answer establishes is
the operative test, which is not 'is this file original'
but **'if I deleted this file, could the code regenerate
it?'**

If yes, it is derived. If no, it is raw, and it needs a
provenance record and a checksum, because nothing in the
compendium can reconstruct it.

Two ambiguous cases arise often enough to expect them. The
first is a **cleaned extract received from a data
coordinating center**. It is derived from someone's raw
data, but not from anything in this compendium, so it is
raw here: your code cannot regenerate it. The rule is that
the boundary is drawn at the edge of *this* compendium, not
at the edge of the world. The second is a **manually
corrected file**, where an analyst fixed a handful of
values by hand. It is not regenerable, because the
corrections live nowhere but in the file, so it must be
treated as raw. The better resolution is to make it derived
by recording the corrections as code, a lookup table of
overrides applied by a script, which restores
regenerability and makes the corrections reviewable.

A third case worth naming is a **cached expensive
computation**, a model that took a day to fit. It is
derived by the test, since the code can regenerate it, but
storing it is sensible. It belongs in `derived_data/` and
should be regenerable on demand rather than trusted
indefinitely.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 3

`R CMD check` is universal because it is the one gate that
applies to every archetype regardless of deliverable. A
manuscript, a simulation, a blog, and a package all carry
the same skin, functions in `R/` that must load, declared
dependencies that must resolve, and tests that must pass,
and `R CMD check` verifies exactly those three things
without knowing or caring what the project produces. The
archetype-specific gates, rendering a document and
checking seed determinism, apply to some archetypes and
not others; this one applies to all of them.

A complete answer also states the limit. The check runs on
the built package, and `.Rbuildignore` excludes
`analysis/`, so it never parses or runs the analysis
scripts. A script there can carry a syntax error or an
undeclared package and the check still passes. 'Universal'
means it applies to every archetype, not that it covers
every file; the analysis code is gated by the render gate
and the dependency scan of @sec-verification.

What the R-package skin buys over a well-named folder is
**an existing verification apparatus that the project
becomes eligible for**. A plain folder can hold all five
artifacts and can in principle reach any rung of the
ladder, so the skin buys nothing in terms of capture. What
it buys is that `DESCRIPTION` and `NAMESPACE` are the
interface `R CMD check` expects, and supplying that
interface makes a large, mature, externally maintained body
of checks apply to your analysis for free. Without it there
is no single standard command that verifies the code loads
and the dependencies resolve, and the analyst must assemble
an equivalent by hand, differently, for every project.

The ceremony is the price of the interface, and the
interface is what makes the tooling apply. This is the
same bargain as any other standard format: the structure is
arbitrary in itself and valuable because other things
already understand it.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 4

A serviceable trajectory has three transitions.

**Simulation study.** The seed-determinism gate is active,
since the results are draws and their reproducibility
depends on the generator. `R CMD check` and unit tests are
active, as always. The render gate is inactive: there is no
document yet.

**Simulation study plus a report on its findings.** The
render gate becomes active. Seeding stays active, since the
simulation still runs. Nothing else changes.

**R package, the simulation logic extracted into exported
functions.** The render gate becomes inactive again if the
report is dropped, or stays active if a vignette replaces
it, which is the usual outcome. Seed determinism becomes
inactive as a *project* gate and reappears inside the unit
tests, as an assertion that a seeded function returns a
recorded value. `R CMD check` becomes more demanding rather
than newly applicable: it now checks documentation
completeness and export consistency, which were vacuous
when nothing was exported.

No directory needs reorganizing at any transition, and this
is the point of the exercise. `R/` held the functions
throughout; it merely gains `@export` tags. `analysis/`
held the driver and the report; it empties or becomes
`vignettes/`. `tests/` gains cases. The Five Pillars are
untouched, because the reproducibility machinery does not
depend on the archetype. What changes is which gates fire,
and gates are configuration rather than structure.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 5

**At best L2.** The compendium can pin its packages with a
lockfile and its environment with a container, so nothing
stops it reaching the second rung. What it cannot do is
reach L3.

**Why not, even in principle.** L3 means the recorded
outputs have been shown to regenerate, within a stated
tolerance, from a clean rebuild. Without a seed, the
generator is initialized from a source that varies between
sessions, so every run draws a different sample and
produces different numbers. There is nothing stable to
compare a rerun against. The failure is not that the
verification is hard or expensive; it is that the property
being verified does not exist. An unseeded simulation has
no recorded output that a rerun could match, so the L3
check is undefined rather than merely unperformed.

Note that the analysis may be perfectly good statistics.
With enough replicates the Monte Carlo error is small and
two runs agree to within it. But 'agrees to within Monte
Carlo error' is a different and weaker claim than 'produces
the recorded outputs to numerical tolerance', and it is the
latter that L3 names.

**A one-line gate.** The cheapest form asserts that the
driver sets a seed at all. `tinytest` runs each test file
with `inst/tinytest/` as the working directory, so the path
climbs two levels to the project root, and the guard lets
the file exit quietly under `R CMD check`, where
`analysis/` is not part of the built package:

```r
driver <- '../../analysis/scripts/run_sim.R'
if (!file.exists(driver)) exit_file('analysis/ not present')
expect_true(
  any(grepl('set\\.seed\\(', readLines(driver))),
  info = 'the simulation driver sets a seed'
)
```

That is a structural check and it is worth saying so: it
confirms the call is present, not that the results are
stable. Running the simulation twice in one session and
asserting the results agree is not the stronger gate
either: both runs share the same R and the same generator
defaults, so a change to those moves both runs together
and the assertion still holds. The stronger gate is a
baseline test (@sec-testing): run the reduced simulation
once, save its summary to a committed baseline file, and
have a `test-baseline-*.R` file recompute the summary in
each later session and compare it with
`expect_equal(..., tolerance = 1e-8)`. That is the
comparison L3 requires, and it costs a great deal more to
run than the one-line check.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 6

**The strongest version of the opposing argument.** A
rendered document is the only artifact that forces the
analyst to state what the analysis *found*. Code and tests
establish that the computation runs and is internally
consistent; neither compels an interpretation. A document
binds a claim to the numbers that support it, and because
it is rendered rather than typed, the binding cannot
silently decay. Requiring one of every compendium would
therefore catch a whole class of failure that gates cannot
see: an analysis that runs perfectly and that nobody has
ever had to summarize, in which an implausible number sits
unremarked because no sentence was ever written next to it.
The render gate would become universal, which is
simplifying, and every project would carry a
human-readable entry point, which is exactly what an
adopter of someone else's compendium most wants.

**Where the argument fails.** It conflates the deliverable
with the interpretation. For an R package, the deliverable
*is* the behavior of the exported functions, and that
behavior is bound to its claims by unit tests, which assert
what the function should return in a form that is checked
on every build. The tests are the binding artifact, and
they are a stronger binding than prose because they are
executable. Requiring a rendered document in addition would
add an artifact that no consumer of the package reads and
that must be maintained in parallel with the tests, which
is how documents drift out of date. The argument also
proves too much: taken seriously it makes reproducibility a
property of documents rather than of re-execution, and a
package with no document but a complete, passing test
suite is plainly more reproducible than a beautifully
rendered report with no tests.

The synthesis the chapter would offer is that every
compendium needs an artifact binding claims to
computation, and that a rendered document is one such
artifact rather than the only one.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 7

```r
raw <- load_cohort('analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv')
cohort <- clean_cohort(raw)
nrow(raw)
#> [1] 338
nrow(cohort)
#> [1] 337
pillars <- c(
  file.exists('Dockerfile'),
  file.exists('renv.lock'),
  file.exists('.Rprofile')
)
sum(pillars)
#> [1] 1
```

**The three numbers**, run against the extract and the
repository as committed: the raw extract holds 338 rows;
the cleaned cohort holds 337; and of the three pillars
checked directly by this script, only `.Rprofile` is
present, so one of three. Counting the source-code pillar
(satisfied by `R/cohort.R` under version control) and the
data pillar (satisfied by the committed raw extract) as
also present, which the script above does not check but
'The cohort, continued' does, brings the total to three of
the Five Pillars, with `Dockerfile` and `renv.lock` absent.
A reader who gets a different row count has either an
edited extract or a different `clean_cohort()` than the
one shipped with this book.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 8

The compendium sits at **L0, locatable**, and no further.

The pillar count from Exercise 7, three of five present,
does not translate into a fraction of a rung because the
ladder of @sec-levels is not a tally across the Five
Pillars; it is a cumulative scale keyed to two specific
artifacts. L1 requires `renv.lock` specifically, and L2
requires an environment recipe specifically, such as a
`Dockerfile`. Both are absent here, so neither L1 nor L2 is
reached regardless of how many of the other three pillars
are present. The session-configuration pillar
(`.Rprofile`), the source-code pillar, and the data pillar
being captured is exactly what L0 already asks for,
locatable code and data under version control, so three
pillars present and L0 reached are the same fact stated
twice, not partial credit toward L1. A compendium cannot
be 'sixty percent of the way' to pinned packages; either
the lockfile exists or it does not.
:::

## Cheat sheet {#sec-cheat-compendium}

| Command or rule | What it does or checks |
|---|---|
| `DESCRIPTION`, `NAMESPACE`, `R/` | The minimal R-package skin; makes a directory checkable by `R CMD check` |
| `.Rbuildignore` entry `^analysis$` | Excludes `analysis/` from the built tarball; `R CMD check` never sees it |
| The Five Pillars | `Dockerfile` (environment), `renv.lock` (packages), `.Rprofile` (session), version control (source code), inclusion or a resolvable identifier (data) |
| 'If I deleted this file, could the code regenerate it?' | The operative test for the raw-versus-derived boundary |
| Five archetypes | Data analysis, scholarly manuscript, R package, simulation study, blog: one skin, differing gates |
| Progressive disclosure | One directory layout carries a project through every archetype with no reorganization |
| Rule of thumb | Name the archetype from the deliverable (a document, a function, stored results, a post), never from the subject matter or the project's size |
| Habit 7 | Write the honest level down: a tidy compendium is a precondition for reproducibility, not evidence of it |

## Further reading

The foundational proposal is Gentleman and Temple Lang's
account of the compendium as an executable document
combining text, code, and data [@gentleman2007]; it reads
well alongside Knuth's original statement of literate
programming, from which the idea descends [@knuth1984]. The
operationalization that this chapter builds on is Marwick,
Boettiger, and Mullen's proposal that an R package is the
natural compendium container, together with their `rrtools`
tool [@marwick2018]. The reader who wants the R-package
mechanics in full should consult Wickham's book on R
packages, which is the standard reference for the skin that
makes `R CMD check` apply [@wickham2015]. For the
complementary skill of *reading* a compendium one has
received rather than writing one, Nust, Boettiger, and
Marwick offer a short and practical guide [@nust2018].
Finally, Peng's argument that reproducibility is a minimum
standard for computational science supplies the motivation
that the compendium is built to serve [@peng2011], and the
individual pillars named in this chapter are developed in
@sec-dependencies, @sec-containers, and the validation
chapters that follow.
